title: Issy Wood selected as first artist in National Portrait Gallery’s new Focus program.
summary: Issy Wood has been selected as the inaugural artist for Artist Focus, a new contemporary program launched by London’s National Portrait Gallery (NPG) dedicated to artists who push the boundaries of portraiture . The program will present three solo displays each year, supported by the Gallery’s newly established Contemporary Council. “Issy Wood: Self-Portraits,” on view October 9, 2026, through February 28, 2027, in the Gallery’s Weston Wing, will bring together 12 self-portraits by the artist, the first and largest presentation devoted to this side of her practice. The exhibition will be free to enter. A standout of the show promises to be Self Portrait 2 (2021), one of three works already in the NPG's collection—the only national institution to hold a Wood self-portrait. The exhibition will also include 11 paintings drawn from the artist’s own collection, seven of which have never been publicly exhibited. Begun in 2020, Wood’s self-portrait series is marked by tight cropping and framing that alternately reveals and obscures the self. The artist has described the paintings as functioning as substitutes for photographs of herself, with the painted image standing in for the real one. “The Gallery’s history has always been one of innovation. We were the first portrait gallery in the world when we were founded in 1856 and remain the global centre for the study and appreciation of portraiture today,” said Dr. Flavia Frigeri, the NPG's chief curator, in a statement. “As the home of portraiture, the NPG is best placed to be a venue and a platform for continued experimentation, as we work to inspire future generations by showcasing the work of trailblazing artists.” Born in North Carolina in 1993, Wood studied at Goldsmiths and the Royal Academy Schools in London and has become known for psychologically charged paintings that draw on personal archives, social media, auction catalogues, and advertising. Her work probes intimacy, desire, and consumer culture, often blurring the line between portraiture, still life , and psychological narrative. Her work is held in the collections of the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris, the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles, the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Denmark, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, and Britain’s Tate, among others. Self-portraiture has featured prominently in Wood’s recent institutional exhibitions, including “Fish, Fish, Duck” at Norway’s Kistefos Museum , now on view through October 11, 2026— her first major presentation in the Nordic region . This exhibition pairs large- and small-format self-portraits with her signature paintings of animals and household objects on velvet-stretched canvas. Other recent high-profile projects for Wood include her portrait of Charli XCX for the cover of Vanity Fair ’s November 2025 art issue and “Magic Bullet,” a recent solo show at Berlin's Schinkel Pavillon.

title: What Sold at Frieze Seoul 2026
summary: Frieze Seoul wrapped up its fifth—and largest—edition on Saturday, September 5th, bringing 133 galleries to the COEX exhibition center in Gangnam. On the floor below, partner fair Kiaf SEOUL 2026 ran concurrently with 175 exhibitors. Yet the more than 300 booths inside COEX represented only a fraction of the art activity unfolding across Seoul—and South Korea more broadly—during the week. Biennials in Gwangju, Jeju, and Busan coincided with the fairs, while the capital hosted a packed program of gallery events, museum exhibitions, and institutional openings, making for one of the most concentrated art weeks anywhere in the world. Nightly neighborhood events centered on galleries and museums brought late openings, parties, and pop-ups to the city, often running well into the night. Major institutional highlights included a Yoo Youngkuk retrospective at the Seoul Museum of Art and the largest-ever survey of Do Ho Suh at MMCA Seoul, which is breaking attendance records, according to the museum. Suh and Yoo were among several artists with major institutional moments who also had a strong presence at Frieze Seoul. Kukje Gallery ’s sale of a 1971 painting by Yoo for ₩2.2–₩2.5 billion ($1.6–$1.85 million) marked the highest price recorded for a Korean artist at the fair since its launch in 2022 and the most expensive reported transaction at this year’s edition. Works by Suh at Lehmann Maupin (one of Artsy’s best booths from the fair ), meanwhile, reportedly sold out quickly. “Seoul’s art scene has its own momentum,” said fair director Patrick Lee. “This week, collectors and institutions came from more countries than at any previous edition, and galleries at the fair made sales across price points, from emerging artists to Korean modern masters.” Across its four-day run, Frieze Seoul drew more than 70,000 visitors, alongside representatives from 178 museums and institutions across 25 countries—a record for the fair. Next year, Frieze Seoul will relocate to the Zaha Hadid –designed Dongdaemun Design Plaza while COEX undergoes renovations. Kiaf will remain at COEX. title: 8 Must-See Shows at Berlin Art Week 2026
summary: Berlin Art Week is back, which officially signals the end of the months of Aperol spritzes, pool trips, and pretending the heat wasn’t unbearable. A slow August can be great, but now it’s time for the city to get back in the groove with some fresh shows. And this year’s return—its 15th edition no less—is not messing around. Big names, rising talent, exhibitions, performances, readings, concerts: If it exists in the art world, it's happening somewhere in Berlin this week. A few examples to watch out for: Maurizio Cattelan is taking over the Neue Nationalgalerie, his first major solo in Germany , after winning the Preis der Nationalgalerie 2026. At Hamburger Bahnhof , musician and actor Ryuichi Sakamoto is finally getting the retrospective he deserves, a European first for this icon. Meanwhile, Schinkel Pavillon and n.b.k. are joining forces on “Projections Onto the East,” exploring the significance of “East” and “West” as concepts in art. And as the art world returns, it’s also saying goodbye: This week marks the final events at Julia Stoschek Collection ’s Berlin location, including a screening by American filmmaker Matt Lambert , and a Spike Art Magazine roundtable on the current state of the arts. Every year Berlin Art Week has to top what it did last time. This year, it actually might. So to save you from full decision paralysis, here are eight must-see gallery shows to get you started. Walter Dahn “Let’s Get Married, Let’s Get Lost” Sprüth Magers Sep. 11–Oct. 24, 2026 There’s a fitting symmetry to this survey at Sprüth Magers, a gallery that started in Cologne in the 1980s, the same scene where Walter Dahn made his name as a founding member of Mülheimer Freiheit—the neo-expressionist group behind "Bad Painting,” where raw brushwork and expressive composition was set deliberately against the precision of Minimalism and Conceptualism . He enrolled at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf at just 17, one of the youngest students to study under Joseph Beuys . Organized with his estate, this is the first exhibition of his work since his death in 2024, spanning 1982 to 2014 and tracking an artist who never settled on a single medium. By 1984 he'd broken from painting almost entirely, turning to silkscreen, which he described as a marriage of photography and painting. Here, he reduces subjects like violence and oppression into small, deliberately spare, reproducible signs, as in Weltkriegshirsch (1984/85). Later in the decade he turned to photography drawn from ethnographic museum displays and mass media; in Untitled (Ex Voto) (1987), Brazilian ex-voto offerings sourced from photocopied photographs are enlarged and recreated by hand, retaining an uncanny presence despite the layers of reproduction. “Animal Mirror” carlier | gebauer Sep. 10–Nov. 14 Few relationships are as old and as unresolved as the one between humans and animals—throughout human history, animals have been seen as companions and confidants, as well as food sources and sacrificial objects, roles that sit uncomfortably close together. In this show , 15 artists take on that contradiction from very different angles, considering animals as part of a shared ecological and genetic system, cohabitants of the same planet and gene pool, and more closely related to us than most people assume. For example, Aki Inomata creates semitransparent shells for hermit crabs, built from the shapes the crabs need to survive, unsettling the idea of human authorship outright. Elsewhere, sculptures by the late German artist Lin May Saeed show her lifelong view of animals as our equals, taking on empathy and liberation directly. In these artworks, tenderness and violence, science and myth all come together, coexisting. “Exquisite Corpse” Pace Gallery Sep. 10–Nov. 11 The title of this exhibition suggests something bleaker than what’s on view. The name is rather borrowed from the Surrealist parlor game , in which each player contributes to a drawing of a body while seeing only the fragment left visible by the last person, a fitting structure for a show about how artists absorb influence without ever seeing the full picture. The show is curated by the artist Loie Hollowell , and it began as a personal tribute to her long-running appreciation for Kiki Kogelnik , the Austrian American Pop artist whose influence still rarely gets the credit it deserves. In conversation with two of her contemporaries, Sascha Braunig and Veronika Pausova , Hollowell realized Kogelnik had shaped all of their practices in strikingly similar ways and built the exhibition around that shared, largely unspoken lineage. Kogelnik’s Cold Passage (1964), where abstract outlines of bodies spread from all sides of the canvas in greens and yellows, serves as a reference point. Hollowell’s Mother Radar in green and orange (2026) shows the most obvious influence, where bodiless arms also reach down from the top of the canvas, to a floating head amid a circular geometric pattern. Katharina Sieverding “ Life-Death ” Galerie Thomas Schulte Sep. 11–Nov. 7 Katharina Sieverding , born in Prague in 1944, has spent more than four decades building a body of autobiographical photographic work centered on identity, gender, and her own shifting social role. This show goes back to where that career effectively started: the 1969 film that gives the show its name, a 29-minute work shot on 16mm and shown here alongside large-format stills and previously unpublished Polaroids. It’s early Sieverding, made in West Berlin during a period of concentrated political and aesthetic upheaval, and it marks a shift away from her earlier theatrical training toward the independent visual language that would define everything she made afterward. The film was significant enough at the time to land Sieverding a place in Documenta 5 three years later, in 1972. She made the film while studying under Joseph Beuys at the Staatliche Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, shooting shortly after the academy’s temporary closure during protests she took part in as both documentarian and participant. The soundtrack deserves its own mention on top of that. An earlier version of the film used spoken text but fell flat; in 1972 it was rescored by the musicians of Kraftwerk , recorded in a single improvised session that catches them mid-transition between rock, experimental sound, and the electronic music they’d soon be known for. Sabine Moritz “ROT GELB BLAU STAUB” Galerie Max Hetzler Sep. 11–Oct. 31 German painter Sabine Moritz ’s first exhibition with Galerie Max Hetzler is a substantial one: 12 large canvases in groups of three, her first quadriptych, still life, and a selection of works on paper upstairs spanning 30 years of practice. Born in Quedlinburg, Germany, in 1969, Moritz surfaces her East German childhood directly in her early work: a series of over 100 pencil drawings of the Neulobeda apartment complex, made in the early 1990s and rediscovered in her studio nearly two decades later by curator Hans Ulrich Obrist . It’s the same material that runs through the works on paper in this show. The upper-floor works trace her earlier method—compositions built from photographs and newspaper cuttings. Over the past decade her paintings have shifted toward intuitive, sketch-free abstraction, and the 12 new works follow that path, loosely structured around the elements of fire, air, earth, and water. These four groups of three canvases each carry something of its element in title, palette, and handling. David Claerbout “ Repose ” Esther Schipper Sep. 10–Oct. 31 Eagle Eye, 2026 David Claerbout Esther Schipper Belgian artist David Claerbout has spent his career playing with time: slowing it down, running it backward, stretching it out until a scene stops feeling like a fixed image and starts to feel alive. His second show with the gallery is staged in a darkened space and brings together four video works, all Berlin premieres, plus a group of related drawings. Walk in and you’ll likely see The woodcarver and the forest (2025) first: a man calmly whittling spoon after spoon, peaceful right up until you notice the forest outside his window is quietly getting smaller with every one he makes. Birdcage (2023) sits nearby, showing the manicured gardens of a stately home taken over by sudden, unexplained violence. Eagle Eye (2026), built from found footage, CGI, and AI, shows a bald eagle strapped to an operating table, awake and staring back, flipping the usual symbol of freedom. And in Backwards Growing Tree (2023), a tree in the Italian countryside, filmed over five years, grows in reverse, so slowly you barely notice something’s wrong. Three of the four works run for hours or years, not minutes, moving at the pace of something alive rather than a usual film. Budget real time if you want to actually sit with them instead of just walking past. Ersan Mondtag “Dispair” DITTRICH & SCHLECHTRIEM Sep. 9–Oct. 31 Ersan Mondtag came to international attention with his artwork Monument of an Unknown Man (2024), when he represented Germany at the Venice Biennale in 2024 , filling the pavilion with a colossal, multistory labyrinth of cramped rooms coated entirely in somber gray asbestos-like dust. This haunting, immersive environment for performers referenced his own family’s migration history. His first solo show with DITTRICH & SCHLECHTRIEM extends that inquiry into a new medium: He uses memory and the body as a historical archive, to create sculptures made almost entirely of wood. In large sculptures, it’s charred, while elsewhere reliefs combine the material with silicone. The choice is deeply conceptual—burning is destruction and preservation at once, a process that mirrors how memory gets physically carried and altered in the body over time. Mondtag’s contribution to Art Week doesn’t stop there. Running alongside the exhibition’s opening, the artist also presents Alternde Meister (2026), a performance at the Gemäldegalerie developed with curator Nadim Samman and produced with the Berliner Ensemble theater group. The performance brings a group of aging performers into dialogue with centuries-old paintings, placing their bodies alongside the museum’s collection and creating a brief encounter between theater and art within the gallery spaces. Xavier Robles de Medina “SOURCE” Galerie Noah Klink Sep. 10–Oct. 10 At Galerie Noah Klink , there’s another gallery debut, and one with a strong personal thread running through it. Born in Suriname in 1990 and now based between his home country and Berlin, Xavier Robles de Medina comes from a family with its own complicated relationship to public history. His grandfather, the sculptor Stuart Robles de Medina, created the 12-foot bronze of former Surinamese prime minister Johan Adolf Pengel that still stands in the capital, Paramaribo’s Independence Square. He was also the one who, on the eve of Surinamese independence in 1975, removed the smaller statue of the Dutch queen Wilhelmina that had also stood in the square. That attention to which figures get memorialized, and which gets quietly forgotten, runs directly through the grandson’s work. For “SOURCE,” the artist uses a research-driven method, pulling from colonial archives, media imagery, and pop culture. He then combines the results to produce hyperrealistic or futuristic-looking paintings and sculptures, which are shown alongside documentary material. The works depict figures caught between human presence and technological or cinematic imagery. One portrays Zoe Saldaña during the making of Avatar: Fire and Ash , her face marked by facial-tracking dots and machinery; another is a stark reproduction of Prince Andrew’s paparazzi shot after he was released from custody. By placing contemporary celebrity imagery alongside documentary sources and technological processes, the artist blurs the boundary between reality and representation, questioning how images shape our understanding of people, events, and truth. title: 5 Standout Shows to See at Small Galleries This September
summary: Mano ultramar, 2026 Juana Gonzalez Arma Gallery Matière noire, 2026 Mathieu Cherkit Semiose In this monthly roundup, we spotlight five stellar exhibitions at small and rising galleries. Juana González “ Manos de hacer ” Arma Gallery , Madrid Sep. 10–Oct. 10 Apoyo en chico ultramar, 2026 Juana Gonzalez Arma Gallery Hands are notoriously hard to paint, the Achilles’ heel of many otherwise capable artists. Spanish artist Juana González has audaciously made the difficult subject matter the central focus of “ Manos de hacer ,” her new exhibition at Arma Gallery in Madrid. Known for her expressive figurative paintings that teeter toward the Baroque, González has frequently used hands as a mode of conveying emotion and dramatic tension. But the artist never noticed the power of hands in her compositions until other artists pointed it out to her. Now, in just over a dozen recent paintings, González homes in on hands in a series of electrically colorful paintings centered on knobby, powerful-looking hands. In one painting, Apoyo en chico ultramar (2026), four red, muscular hands grasp the two shoulders of a young man who casts a faraway glance. In another, Pelo (2022), two massive hands stroke the hair of a young woman. González holds a degree in fine arts from the Complutense University of Madrid, and her work has been exhibited at institutions including the Cervantes Institute in Munich, Centro de Arte Alcobendas, and the Museum of the University of Alicante. Mark Francis “ Chroma ” Bernhard Knaus Fine Art , Frankfurt, Germany Sep. 4–Nov. 21 Strata, 2026 Mark Francis Bernhard Knaus Fine Art What if color had a sound? In a new exhibition , Northern Irish painter Mark Francis creates abstract paintings that treat color as a kind of audio frequency. In 16 paintings, vertical stripes of color zip down the canvases, with small, glitchlike alterations reminiscent of printer banding. Francis overlaps, echoes, and layers these marks, creating compositions that look like you should be able to hear them. Works such as Audio Division II and Scaler (both 2026) underscore these sonic sensibilities in their titles without ever being too specific. The works thrive in these spaces of recognition and dissolution. Over the past 30 years, Francis has established a painting practice closely aligned with science. His wet-on-wet paintings have explored theories of chaos and order, astronomy, and his own personal interest in mycology—the study of fungi. Francis studied painting at Central Saint Martins, followed by Chelsea College of Arts, where he completed his MA in painting in 1986. His works are in the collections of the Irish Museum of Modern Art and the Tate. Francis’s work is also currently on view in “Sea of Sound ” for the Republic of San Marino at the 2026 Venice Biennale . Olayami Dabls “ Looking Back ” Matéria Gallery , Detroit Sep. 11–Oct. 31 Looking Back #3, 2025 Olayami Dabls Matéria Gallery In this show , Detroit artist and cultural historian Olayami Dabls debuts nine new large-scale wall works made in 2025 and 2026. Born in 1948, Dabls is known in Detroit as “the bead man”; he founded the Dabls Mbad African Bead Museum in 2004, an art campus dedicated to preserving and presenting African material culture and heritage. The artist’s own works incorporate materials found locally, and in this show he uses iron, rocks, wood, and mirrors for their associations with certain healing properties. Iron, for instance, acts as a metaphor for abundance, strength, and advancement. Mirrors, in African culture, can be used to repel negative energies. These mixed-media works draw from the heritages of African material culture, Detroit’s urban landscape, and Dabls’s personal symbology. Earlier this year, Dabls presented his first museum retrospective, “Detroit Cosmologies,” at the Museum of Contemporary Art Detroit (MOCAD). In 2022, he was named the Kresge Eminent Artist for his lifetime of excellence in the arts and community service in Detroit. Mathieu Cherkit “ Tendrement ” Semiose , Paris Through Oct. 31 Tendrement, 2026 Mathieu Cherkit Semiose French artist Mathieu Cherkit draws inspiration from close to home—literally. The artist is best known for his paintings of the house where he lives with his family. In his first exhibition at Semiose , Cherkit presents 15 new paintings centered on this subject. His methods are both precise and inventive: Cherkit paints each section of his paintings at set times of day. One corner might be painted every morning, another in late afternoon, until the painting is complete. He works from sketches, but also from memory, and playfully rearranges perspectives and proportions in ways he finds interesting. The painting Matière Noire (2026), for instance, shows a saucepan filled with eggs in a few inches of water, cooking on a stovetop. Seemingly straightforward at first, the painting is a perspectival riddle, with the burner, grate, pan, and knobs all painted from differing angles, in a nod to the Cubist approach. Born in 1982, the artist lives and works in Vallery, France. He graduated from the Nantes School of Fine Arts and the Hochschule für Grafik und Buchkunst in Leipzig, Germany. His work is included in the collections of Paris’s Centre National des Arts Plastiques and the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris. Bang Soyun and Jaiyoung Cho “ mine ” SPACE SO , Seoul Through Sep. 12 Body Module, 2026 Jaiyoung Cho SPACE SO The Layers - Piercing #1, 2026 Bang Soyun SPACE SO Korean contemporary artists Bang Soyun and Jaiyoung Cho grapple with the body, individuality, and questions of collapse and collision in this dual exhibition spanning painting and mixed-media sculpture. Bang Soyun’s oil-and-acrylic paintings are uncanny arrangements of entrails, bones, and eyes. In her painting The Layers - Piercing #1 (2026), these skeletal forms teeter atop one another like a precarious sculptural form. Soyun also brings these subjects into three dimensions with small-scale sculptures made from acrylic, sand, and plastic. The artist, born in 1992, uses 3D modeling software and AR to visualize these creations. Jaiyoung Cho, meanwhile, presents works in sculpture and installation made with materials such as cardboard, metal, thread, and fabric. These forms are flexible in format, made through layering, cutting, and arrangement, often in response to their architectural surroundings. Works from the series “Body Module” are small-scale, colorful wall pieces, each an open, framelike form with a dangling pendant suspended from a chain. Other works from the “Body & Bodies” series are freestanding sculptures reminiscent of room dividers, but often with cutouts or openings that draw attention to the gallery space instead. Born in 1979, Jaiyoung Cho received her BFA and MFA in sculpture from Ewha Womans University in Seoul and an MA in fine art from the Utrecht School of the Arts in the Netherlands. Her work has been exhibited at galleries including Wooson Gallery and Carvalho , as well as institutions including the Kumho Museum of Art and Atelier Hermès.

title: The 10 Best Booths at Frieze Seoul 2026
summary: The fifth edition of Frieze Seoul opened at the COEX in Gangnam on Wednesday, September 2nd, hosting 133 galleries from 30 countries. By the start of the fair’s VIP opening at 11 a.m., three lines poured out of the entrances, with visitors moving as frenetically as South Korea’s stock market. The energy was high, and it continued throughout the day. Returning international heavyweight exhibitors such as Hauser & Wirth and Pace Gallery were joined by Seoul mainstays Gallery Hyundai and Kukje Gallery , which mounted thoughtfully curated presentations. Still, many exhibitors appeared to hedge their bets with painting-heavy booths anchored by a statement sculpture. More consequential were this year’s curatorial shifts. Replacing Frieze Masters, Spotlight revisited overlooked 20th-century practices, while Material Practice brought together ceramics, textiles, glass, metal, wood, and paper. Focus, the section dedicated to younger galleries, expanded beyond Asia for the first time, presenting 16 emerging galleries likely to appeal to newer collectors. Several galleries also timed their selections to Korea’s packed institutional calendar, including Koo Jeong A ’s Leeum, Samsung Museum of Art solo, Do Ho Suh ’s MMCA survey, as well as several other names featured in the current Gwangju and Busan biennials. Alongside a week of “Neighborhood Nights” gallery events and the openings of the Park Seo-Bo Museum and Seo-Seoul Museum of Art, the growth of Korea’s cultural infrastructure was felt across town. Corporate leaders, celebrities, curators, and directors circulated through the aisles on the fair’s VIP day, reflecting the fair’s growing role within Seoul’s cultural ecosystem. On the floor below, partner fair Kiaf SEOUL echoed a similar enthusiasm . By the end of Frieze’s VIP day, several galleries reported high-value transactions, led by Thaddaeus Ropac ’s sale of Adrian Ghenie ’s Figure with Funerary Stele (2026), for €1.1 million ($1.3 million). Read Artsy’s day one Frieze Seoul sales report here , and check back next week for our full roundup. Here, we present the 10 best booths from Frieze Seoul 2026. Lehmann Maupin Booth A25 With works by Do Ho Suh, Kim Yun Shin, Sung Neung Kyung, Guimi You, and others Past a bustling entrance, the first thing visitors encounter is the pale, quiet architecture of Do Ho Suh’s home sculptures at Lehmann Maupin . On the front wall, Perfect Home—Horsham, New York, New York, Sant’Angelo in Pontano… (2026), a translucent polyester work, layers the many places Suh has lived into a single home structure. The booth moves between earlier and recent thread drawings and fabric sculptures from Suh’s “Family Cuddle” and “Scaled Behaviour” series, with a smaller section devoted to works by other gallery artists such as Kim Yun Shin and Guimi You . The Body Shimmer (Trevor, the Wishing), 2026 Dominic Chambers Lehmann Maupin My Heart Is on the Court, 2026 Mr. Lehmann Maupin dna:study, 2025 McArthur Binion Lehmann Maupin The Body Shimmer (Tre, the Passionate), 2026 Dominic Chambers Lehmann Maupin koi carp, 2 botanical gardens LA, 2025 Billy Childish Lehmann Maupin At Night, 2025 Chantal Joffe Lehmann Maupin Add Two Add One Divide Two Divide One 2023-28, 2023 Kim Yun Shin Lehmann Maupin Prayer of the Soul 2014-65, 2014 Kim Yun Shin Lehmann Maupin Unsurprisingly, it was among the VIP day’s hardest booths to enter. Singaporean gallery STPI is also showing Suh’s work elsewhere at the fair, making him one of this edition’s defining presences. While his international reputation has attracted serious collectors for decades, his frequently sold-out MMCA survey that is currently on view appears to have brought in a newer audience, too. Suh’s name kept surfacing in the group chats around me, where people traded messages about barely getting close enough to ask a price. That enthusiasm carried through to sales. “We placed a significant number of works on the preview day, with the majority acquired by Asian clients,” said the gallery’s co-founder Rachel Lehmann. Duarte Sequeira Booth A03 With works by Nell Brookfield, Edmond Brooks-Beckman, André Butzer, Petra Cortright, Tom Howse, Patrick H Jones, Hyunjin Kim, Julian Opie, Paolo Salvador, and Yooyun Yang For its second Frieze Seoul appearance, Portuguese gallery Duarte Sequeira brings together its international and Korean programs. It opened in Seoul four years ago—first in Cheongdam, before moving to Hannam last year—after entering the Korean market through the Kiaf and Art Busan fairs. Its roots run deeper in Portugal , where the Sequeira family has worked with British stalwart Julian Opie for some three decades. Here, the artist’s pared-down figures appear alongside paintings by Korean artists Yooyun Yang and Hyunjin Kim . The booth’s sharpest discovery is London painter Patrick H Jones , whose recent Seoul solo show, “Crowded Emotions,” sold out, according to the gallery. His five new paintings begin with everyday scenes that he cuts apart and recombines into unstable narratives. In Fools again and Fed up again (both 2026), figures sit behind windshields and other barriers, their gestures wavering between comedy and aggression. Jones compares emboldened online behavior to road rage: Both arise from the sense of protection created by a screen. His tightly cropped compositions turn that distance into uneasy studies of how readily judgment becomes distorted. Gaa Gallery Booth F1 With works by Johanna Seidel At a corner of the fair’s Focus section, visitors to Gaa Gallery ’s booth were welcomed by the gallerist—and his eight-month-old son, watching from a stroller. It was a fittingly personal introduction to the pastoral yet slightly surreal paintings of Dresden-based German artist Johanna Seidel . With spaces in Cologne and New York, the gallery is making its Frieze Seoul debut in the section for galleries founded since 2014. This is also Seidel’s first presentation in Korea, following a strong response at Art Basel Hong Kong earlier this year. Look longer, and they drift somewhere between everyday life and dreams. Siennas, violets, and murky greens give the oil paintings an unexpectedly soft, almost porous quality. Most are modest enough to fit above a bed. Jewel Thief (2026), a portrait of a woman holding a cigar on a tall, narrow canvas, is priced at €3,000 ($3,478). While I was there, a collector who had purchased another small painting was already asking whether they could take it home that day. LAMB Booth F11 With works by Ayla Tavares Deeper inside the Focus section, opposite a booth awash in bright color, Brazilian artist Ayla Tavares ’s quiet ceramic installation pulls visitors in. Small, cream-colored objects dot the booth’s three walls like a constellation. At the center, The pineal eye (2026)—a ceramic sculpture fitted with a light mechanism—glows softly from a pedestal. From afar, the presentation feels spare and restrained; up close, its delicate drawings, varied textures, and intricate surfaces reveal themselves. Starting from a Thanaka tablet from Myanmar and Georges Bataille’s short Surrealist text The Solar Anus , the artist uses the notion of the sun to connect body, matter, light, and knowledge. Works are priced between $6,000 and $15,000, with The pineal eye offered at $15,000. The presentation follows the artist’s recent inclusion in a Hammer Museum group show, which gallery founder and director Lucinda Bellm said generated strong interest among L.A. collectors. Tavares will also participate in Brazil’s first pavilion at this month’s Gwangju Biennale. David Zwirner Booth B9 With works by Francis Alÿs, Mamma Andersson, Lucas Arruda, Ruth Asawa, Katherine Bernhardt, Michaël Borremans, Suzan Frecon, Scott Kahn, Yayoi Kusama, Giorgio Morandi, Walter Price, Gerhard Richter, Dana Schutz, Steven Shearer, Rirkrit Tiravanija, Wolfgang Tillmans, Luc Tuymans, and Rose Wylie Anchored by the late Yayoi Kusama centerpiece sculpture, FLOWERS THAT SPEAK ALL ABOUT MY HEART GIVEN TO THE SKY (2018), David Zwirner brought the household names expected from a gallery of its caliber, from Giorgio Morandi and Ruth Asawa to Luc Tuymans . Kusama had passed away just a week before the fair . Alongside neighboring Hauser & Wirth, Zwirner’s booth was a display in which museum curators from around the world seemed most inclined to stop, look, and linger. Sud, 1986 Francis Alÿs David Zwirner Rio Amazonas, Septiembre 22, 2025 Francis Alÿs David Zwirner Behind the Curtain, 2014 Mamma Andersson David Zwirner Pond, 2019 Mamma Andersson David Zwirner Untitled (from the Deserto-Modelo series), 2026 Lucas Arruda David Zwirner Untitled (from the Deserto-Modelo series), 2026 Lucas Arruda David Zwirner Abstraktes Bild (Abstract Painting), 2001 Gerhard Richter David Zwirner The Stage, 2010 Luc Tuymans David Zwirner The Moody Muse, 2025 Steven Shearer David Zwirner Napoleon (Film Notes), 2026 Rose Wylie David Zwirner Vola, 2025 Katherine Bernhardt David Zwirner Shoot!, 2026 Walter Price David Zwirner purple ocher moroccan, 2021 Suzan Frecon David Zwirner Still, its blue-chip familiarity did not make the presentation feel predictable. A delicate 1976 bronze-wire sculpture by Asawa offered a counterpoint to Morandi’s hushed 1942 painting and the louder contemporary works around them. By the end of preview day, the gallery reported placing a significant number of works, including a new Lucas Arruda painting with an Asian museum. “South Korea has a sophisticated collector base with a deep knowledge of Western artists,” said associate partner James Green, noting that many visitors required “little introduction to the works.” Mendes Wood DM Booth B8 With works by Laís Amaral, Lucas Arruda, Eunnam Hong, Josi, Amadeo Luciano Lorenzato, Tomie Ohtake, Precious Okoyomon, Lygia Pape, Marina Perez Simão, Paulo Nazareth, Paulo Nimer Pjota, Mário Rubinski, Luiz Roque, Paula Siebra, Daniel Steegmann Mangrané, and Kishio Suga Returning to Frieze Seoul after sitting out last year, Mendes Wood DM brings a booth that takes a moment to unpack. Lucas Arruda’s monochrome painting recalls deep water at dusk, while Korean painter Eunnam Hong ’s Bomb (2026) places a quiet threat beneath images of luxury and desire. Then there is Precious Okoyomon ’s shy bear sculpture, looking back at the view with its claws out and flames in its eyes, alongside a 1961 “blind painting” by Japanese Brazilian artist Tomie Ohtake . Aguilera noted that the gallery’s Korean collectors are “very loyal” and “very consistent,” but said he still hopes to surprise them with this year’s booth display. Asked what might do so this year, he pointed to works by Amadeo Luciano Lorenzato , once little known even in Brazil, represented here by two small paintings from the 1980s. Axel Vervoordt Gallery Booth B17 With works by Kimsooja, Kim Lim, Shi Zhiying, and Bosco Sodi Kimsooja ’s “Bottari” is what first draws visitors into Axel Vervoordt Gallery ’s booth. Most will recognize the artist’s signature colorful bundle sculpture immediately. The surprise comes when they realize that the nearby ceramics—delicately punctured as if stitched with an invisible thread—are also hers. Seen alongside the light-absorbing black form of Deductive Object , they show how her familiar gestures of wrapping and sewing continue through clay, light, and sculpture. The gallery’s presentation this year feels like an equally seamless transition. As Sabrina Hung of the gallery explained, its earlier program leaned more heavily toward 20th-century practices, while its roster has increasingly expanded into contemporary art. Having previously participated in Frieze Seoul through its Masters section, the gallery now enters the fair’s main section, bringing its historical eye into conversation with that growing contemporary program. Kim Lim ’s sculpture Pegasus (Bronze) (1962) distills the mythical horse into a few upright curves, while new paintings by Shi Zhiying and Bosco Sodi take very different routes through time and texture. Yet the combination feels entirely in character for a gallery long associated with quiet materiality and cross-generational dialogue. Like the booth itself, its roster links tradition and the present without making much noise about it. Works in the presentation range in price from $50,000 to $600,000. drawingRoom Booth C16 With works by Yoo Jung Ellie Choi, Sanoh Lee, Sooji Lee, Leebinsoyeon, Donghoon Rhee, Im Sungoo, Miyeon Yi, and Jinsik Yoo If visitors want to see young Korean artists without being grouped by a single aesthetic, local gallery drawingRoom ’s booth is a highlight stop. unexpected rhythm, while works in paper, thread, and paint extend along the surrounding walls. Visitors would do well to look behind the booth’s partition, where Im’s The Tilted Room (2026), a densely layered paper-based work, waits almost in hiding. Built from compressed paper and graphite, it carries fragments of domestic spaces erased by Korea’s rapid redevelopment. The presentation continues beyond the fair at drawingRoom’s Seoul space, where a related exhibition, “Rigorous Hands,” is on view through September 12th. Gagosian Booth C10 With works by Damien Hirst From Moon Kyungwon and Jeon Joonho ’s nearby seating installation, where tired visitors can take a break, the orderly dots of Damien Hirst ’s “ Spots ” paintings and centrifugal bursts of his “ Spin ” paintings come directly into view. The booth feels like the section’s unofficial anchor. Inside, those instantly recognizable paintings give way to Nemesis (2007), a clinically ordered work from the “Pill Cabinets” series, and faux archaeological relics from the “Treasures from the Wreck of the Unbelievable” series. Hirst’s MMCA survey drew more than 500,000 visitors this spring while also stirring debate over its blockbuster scale, public spending, and critical framing—perhaps fitting for an artist who has never been far from controversy. By the end of the day, the gallery had placed “significant works” from the presentation to collections including a museum in Asia. Indeed, the “Spots” and “Spin” paintings were attracting the most visitors—and camera phones. For anyone wanting to look beyond the spectacle, Gagosian’s detailed online presentation offers short texts and videos on each series. UNAW Gallery Booth S13 With works by Gyutae Hwang Photography is hard to find at Frieze Seoul this year. For its debut at the fair, UNAW Gallery joins the new Spotlight section with Korean artist Gyutae Hwang , tracing his work from the 1960s through the 2000s. The gallery’s executive director, Soyoung Ryu, emphasized Hwang’s historical importance as an early figure who continually tested the boundaries of what photography in Korea could be. Embankment Path, 1960s Hwang Gyutae UNAW Gallery UNTITLED, 1969-1970 Hwang Gyutae UNAW Gallery Myeongdong Cathedral, 1960s Hwang Gyutae UNAW Gallery Burning the City II, 1969 Hwang Gyutae UNAW Gallery Panacea, 2000 Hwang Gyutae UNAW Gallery Blow Up, 1960s Hwang Gyutae UNAW Gallery BIG BANG THEORY, 1995-2000 Hwang Gyutae UNAW Gallery Spring (A Girl Going to Gather Wild Greens), Hongdae, 1960s Hwang Gyutae UNAW Gallery The presentation moves from small black-and-white examples of figurative and representative photography toward images that become increasingly difficult to call photographs at all. For Burning the City II (1969), Hwang physically burned the film, producing an abstraction that resembles fireworks exploding above warped city buildings—at once celebratory and destructive. Later works enlarge, repeat, and digitally distort their source images. Ryu chose Panacea (2000) as her favorite for its sharp social critique and unusual palette. My eyes, however, kept returning to the early photographs, priced at roughly one-seventh as much, at around ₩3 million ($2,205)—especially Myeongdong Cathedral (1960s), a quiet scene that captures the minor dramas of a single day in a rapidly modernizing Korea.

title: Nan Goldin shoots Acne Studios’ 30th anniversary campaign.
summary: Acne Studios has enlisted Nan Goldin to shoot its 30th-anniversary campaign, the Swedish fashion house announced. The American photographer made a series of portraits of artists, musicians, and actors from the brand’s orbit, each dressed in denim—the material the label built its name on—in a mix of new, archival, and reissued styles from its three decades. Goldin photographed nine friends of the house: artists Jonathan Lyndon Chase , Sandra Poulson , and Peter Schlesinger ; actors Rila Fukushima and Juliette Lewis; models Raya Martigny and Guinevere Van Seenus ; musician Ellie Rowsell; and photographer Jordan Hemingway. A 10th portrait, of an unnamed friend, will follow at a later date. All the sitters have worked with the brand before: Chase designed the runway set for its Spring/Summer 2025 show in Paris, and Poulson’s sculptures have appeared in its stores. “I have been inspired by Nan and her work for years,” said Jonny Johansson, co-founder and creative director of Acne Studios, in a statement. “So, when we realized we had 30 years to celebrate, it felt like the right moment to ask her. I wanted an icon, but I also wanted something very intimate and personal. She does that.” The sitters, he added, are “individuals we have collaborated with, spoken to, or had some kind of exchange with over the years. I wanted friends, not models.” The commission is a natural fit for Goldin, who has spent five decades photographing her chosen family of friends and lovers, most famously in “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency ” (1985). In 2017, she founded the group P.A.I.N. , whose museum protests pushed institutions worldwide to drop the Sackler name over the family’s role in the opioid crisis. Laura Poitras ’s documentary All the Beauty and the Bloodshed (2022) chronicled her life and that campaign. Goldin has shot for fashion houses before, including a 2024 Gucci campaign featuring Debbie Harry and Kelsey Lu.

title: The 5 Best Booths at Kiaf SEOUL 2026
summary: Kiaf SEOUL returned to the COEX in Gangnam with a typically stylish and enthusiastic crowd on Wednesday, September 2nd. Marking a milestone 25th anniversary, the fair brings together 175 exhibitors from 18 countries under its first externally appointed creative director, designer Kuho Jung, who oversaw a rebrand built around the theme of Coexistence. This iteration promises an exploration of humanity’s shifting relationship with technology. Special exhibitions “HUMAL” and “Invisible,” the latter woven with AR works accessible by QR codes across the fair floor, extend the theme. Coexistence, it turns out, is built into the fair’s very architecture. This is also the fifth year that Kiaf shares its venue with Frieze Seoul , which takes place on the floor above. The result is a sense of fluidity and buzz; Wednesday’s throng of VIPs flitted between the two. The youthful, engaged, and excited crowd here makes the fairs feel like a festival. At one point, it was difficult to peruse Kiaf’s aisles without ending up in someone’s selfie or video. Works by international heavyweights are plentiful at Kiaf, but visitors can also leave the fair with myriad discoveries, thanks to the strong regional depth in dealers and artists. The organizers have successfully curated a neat snapshot of the Korean and regional art scene, with a smattering of global flair. “It’s the biggest platform for art in Korea,” Sunghoon Lee, the president of the Galleries Association of Korea, which runs the fair, told Artsy. “The fair’s role is to put new artists and older artists together, and Kiaf is the biggest in size, top quality, and it also has the most number of participants in Korea. We also have international galleries participating, so it is a platform for networking.” And art lovers in Seoul will have plenty to feast on beyond the COEX, as if more than 250 gallery booths wasn’t enough. The fairs anchor Seoul Art Week, which brings an enormous serving of shows and pop-ups to town. Each night this week, different neighborhoods take turns hosting a local cluster of events and openings, turning art viewing into a round-the-clock task of trying to avoid FOMO. And if that still wasn’t enough, then consider that this year’s Seoul Art Week is part of the Korea Art Festival. Some four biennales—Jeju, Busan, Gwangju, and Gyeonggi—are all taking place across the country this month, adding firepower to a week in the Korean capital that is already among the busiest in the art world. Indeed, judging by the mood at the COEX, the audience here is more than ready to take on the challenge. Here, we select our five best booths from Kiaf SEOUL 2026. Her work appears alongside that of established Korean artists Lee Kyoungmi , Hanna Kim , Hur BoRee , and Baek Kyungho . Yet it’s Hong’s oil paintings that dominate the space. title: $1.28 million Adrian Ghenie painting leads opening sales at Frieze Seoul 2026.
summary: Frieze Seoul 2026 kicked off its VIP day on Wednesday, September 2nd, at COEX. Now in its fifth edition, the fair is known for drawing a mix of collectors, curators, institutional leaders, and stylish VIPs, largely from across the Asia Pacific region. This year was no exception, with K-pop stars The8 from the band Seventeen and Annie and Bailey from AllDay Project, singer Woodz, models Hye-jin Han and Yano Shiho, and actors Ji-won Uhm, Dasom, So-Hee Han, and Si-young Lee. Adding to the initial excitement were several six-and seven-figure transactions, led by Thaddaeus Ropac ’s sale of Adrian Ghenie ’s Figure with Funerary Stele (2026), for €1.1 million ($1.28 million). “It’s fantastic to see how Seoul Art Week has matured across the city, with the impressive institutional developments and the calibre of museum exhibitions,” said gallery founder Thaddaeus Ropac. “It’s been a strong start to the fair with swift sales, largely to collectors based in Korea, but also spanning Asia—Malaysia, China, Hong Kong—and a few to European and American collectors.” Dealers also reported active institutional buying, particularly from Asia.
